newsitem.title: USA: Crude's price fall saps awaited US gasoline rally.
newsitem.headline: Crude's price fall saps awaited US gasoline rally.

text.p: U.S. automobile drivers may feel less pinched at the pump this summer as a sharp downturn in crude prices has already put the brakes on this spring's seasonal gasoline rally.

"I don't expect this year's gasoline rally to show up on the front page of the newspaper," said Tim Evans, analyst with Pegasus Econometric Research in New York, noting this year's peak in gasoline prices may fall below the 1996 peak.
Gasoline futures on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) typically rally in the beginning of spring, anticipating traditional peak summer demand.
Last year, gasoline rocketed 14 cents a gallon in the first month of spring alone to a new post-Gulf War high of 78.10 cents on supply concerns.

But with spring just a month away, the market has turned bearish amid slack demand for heating oil. The price of light sweet crude on the NYMEX has dropped more than $2.50 a barrel or more than 10 percent in the past seven sessions.
A host of market players said crude may recover only a fraction of its value, restraining the spring gasoline rally.

"I don't think we are going to break last year's levels in gasoline. I think we may not even get to 75.00 cents since crude has seen it's highs," said Thomas Blakeslee, analyst with Cargill Investor Services in New York .
"I think this year we may get a rally to maybe 71.00 cents," said Jeff Foose, trader with KCS Energy in New Jersey.
On Friday, gasoline for March delivery settled at 65.30 cents a gallon.
"We are sort of neutral on gasoline for now," said Todd Miller, vice president and refined products trader at Morgan Stanley in New York.

According to the American Petroleum Institute (API), gasoline supplies at January 31 were 7.4 million barrels below a year ago compared to last year's year-over-year deficit of 6.3 million barrels at that time.
But, rapid refining of readily available crude is expected to swiftly replenish stocks.

In recent weeks, refiners have been given monetary incentive to create gasoline due to the expansion of the crude-to-gasoline crack spread, the difference between crude's price and gasoline's and a part of refiner profitability.
"Refiners have gotten the signal to produce gasoline early with the crack spread," said Morgan Stanley's Miller.
In fact, the API said gasoline stocks increased 4.7 million barrels in the second half of January.
Last year's rally was sharpened by uncertainty over whether the U.N.-Iraq oil-for-food deal would be approved.
But in December, the United Nations allowed Iraq to export oil for the first time since Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait in exchange for humanitarian aid.
Iraqi supply has increased output of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) to a new 16-year high in January, according to a Reuters survey.

Meanwhile, dealers said talk that the gasoline stock deficit could lead to a severe tightness come spring is simply alarmist. They said it echoes the concern of a heating oil shortage heard this past fall.
At that time, refiners were able to quickly restore heat supplies before winter demand by stepping up production. Market players expect the same production efficiency this year with gasoline.
"We had the exact same talk coming into the winter about heating oil, but refiners have proven they can manage their inventories," said KCS Energy's Foose, adding:
"We just don't have the same ingredients as last year. We are sucking up a lot of gasoline cargoes from everywhere it seems."
Indeed, some market players were expecting gasoline imports to approach a historically high 650,000 barrels per day in February due in part to an open arbitrage from Europe in January.
Even the driver's vigilant watchdog, the American Automobile Association (AAA), is encouraged by some easing in supply tightness, although it remains cautious overall.
"We continue to be concerned about tightness of gasoline supply, and we expect it to continue to exert upward pressure on spot prices," said Bill Jackman, AAA spokesman.
"But, we are encouraged by gasoline stocks moving upward, and some analysts are even calling for a surplus by March," he added.
